articles.title: Embraced across divides, Dolly Parton leaves a lasting legacy
articles.summary: Throughout her lifetime, Dolly Parton worked to build a better world, while becoming inextricable from the American imagination. She was embraced by fans across gender, race and class, embodying a mythology typically inaccessible to even the most influential historical figures. It is one of her greatest legacies: to take what you have and help someone with it.
articles.content:
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

There are few inalienable truths: Everyone was born, everyone will die, and everyone loved Dolly Parton.

Larger-than-life at 5-foot-nothing, the country star, actor, philanthropist, entrepreneur and theme park enthusiast who died Tuesday, transcended celebrity in rhinestones and fringe. She was embraced by fans across gender, race and class, embodying a mythology typically inaccessible to even the most influential historical figures.

It’s hard to name a more adored artist – one who could deliver a perfectly timed dirty joke seconds before a folk classic of her own composition. (This is where, if Parton were reading along, a self-deprecating quip would come in – lest anyone forget she was a whip-smart jokester, too.)

Throughout her endeavors, Parton worked to build a better world, while becoming inextricable from the American imagination. It is one of her greatest legacies: to take what you have and help someone with it.

In 2015, when Parton returned to Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium, Grand Ole Opry announcer Bill Cody introduced her as “the most beloved artist of all time,” quickly amending it to “female artist.” As history has proven, he was correct the first time.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement. Accept Manage my choices One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site. Try again Cover image: US singer Dolly Parton - seen here in 2019 - enjoyed a long career in country music and as an actress. © Robyn Beck, AFP/File 02:14

Parton’s legacy starts with the immortality of her music: songwriting as solace, an exercise in creativity and an unwavering ability to write experience into art. Across her career, Parton wrote and performed perennial hits (“Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “Little Sparrow,” take your pick) and others that took on a life of their own (most famously, “I Will Always Love You,” made immortal by Whitney Houston ).

Parton grew up in poverty, one of 12 kids in East Tennessee’s rural Sevier County, where she started writing songs as a toddler. By 10, she was on the radio and TV in Knoxville, Tennessee. By 13, she had made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry. At 21, she joined “The Porter Wagoner Show,” her star power quickly eclipsing its host.

The accomplishments – and the trials and tribulations that came with them, which she let roll off her shoulders with enviable resiliency – came fast and furious, as they do with once-in-a-lifetime talents. There are the 10 Grammys, the numerous Hall of Fame inductions, and the fact that she revolutionized the world of country music for women alongside Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette, creating a path for crossover artistry. But there are also her Hollywood forays. It’s telling that her first feature film, “9 to 5,” celebrated women in the workplace and messed with their devious bosses.

Read moreBeloved US country music icon Dolly Parton dies at 80

One of her superpowers was rooted in a kind of irony: Everything about Dolly Parton is truly Dolly Parton or else she wouldn’t partake — down to the false eyelashes and big wigs. She built an economic empire with down-home sensibilities. If authenticity is currency in popular culture, Parton showed the world how it was done.

There’s a moment in her 1983 television special, “Dolly in Concert,” where Parton calls herself “the original punk rocker.” It’s a fitting description: Armed in a uniform of high heels, acrylic nails (the better to write songs with), tight clothes and big blond beehive, the image of Parton was enough to scandalize. Jokes about her breasts were prevalent for decades; she wielded them like a weapon.

Her first big break came in 1967 with a single, ironically titled “Dumb Blonde.” It’s a clever admonishment of a man who calls a woman stupid. It was fabulously misunderstood and misconstrued, forecasting the wonderful hypocrisy inherent in many public appreciations of Parton: She had full autonomy; make a low-brow pass at her and she’ll have the last laugh. Always.

That spirit was inherent in her business ventures as well. Too poor to travel to Disneyland as a child, Parton opened her Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, amusement park, Dollywood, in 1986. Many thought it was a bad idea; it proved to be her most lucrative business venture. It’s also, crucially, a blessing for the local economy. According to a 2021 study by the Tennessee Aviation System Plan, Dollywood brings in $1.8 billion each year.

Read moreFrench DJ Kavinsky, famed for 'Nightcall', dies at 50

Parton’s career kicked off in the transformative ’60s, perfectly aligning with the emergence of the women’s liberation movement. Though she didn’t use the word herself, much of Parton’s career – and in particular, her songwriting – has been viewed as a kind of feminism. Take the early hit, 1968’s “Just Because I’m a Woman.” Parton’s sweet soprano and idiosyncratic tremolo are on full display as she reminds her male partner that he need not judge her for having previous sexual partners because he has done the same. “My mistakes are no worse than yours,” she sings, “Just because I’m a woman.”

Or consider 1970's “Down from Dover,” a tearjerker about a pregnant teenager abandoned by her family and the child’s father. She gives birth to a stillborn baby, alone, without medical treatment. “I guess in some strange way she knew she’d never have a father’s arms to hold her,” Parton sings. “And dying was her way of telling me he wasn’t coming down from Dover.” It’s evocative then and now.

Still, across political divides, Parton is welcomed with open arms. It may have something to do with the fact that, when it came to capital-P party line, Parton valued apoliticism. During the 2016 presidential election, she said a woman would do a great job in office. When it was viewed as an endorsement of Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton, she said her words were taken out of context. She never said who she voted for. And she declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times, twice from President Donald Trump and once from President Joe Biden so as to not appear biased. As a result, she was beloved by all — even in periods of unmitigated division.

Try again Cover image: © France 24 07:46

With the same resolve she exhibited in her performances, Parton was dedicated to charity work.

In 1988, she launched the Dollywood Foundation, originally designed to combat high school dropout rates. Its early '90s Buddy Program paired junior high students in Sevier County and gave $500 to each if they both finished high school. In 2016, when wildfires ravaged her native Great Smoky Mountains, the foundation announced it would give $1,000 each month for six months to families who lost their homes. The following year, it was revealed the foundation’s My People Fund helped 900 families with roughly $9 million in the first six months after the fires.

In 1991, she launched a sanctuary for bald eagles that couldn't survive in the wild; in 2000, she started a college scholarship giving $15,000 to five high school seniors in Sevier County. In 2020, she donated $1 million to COVID-19 research at Vanderbilt University, which helped fund Moderna’s vaccine.

Best known is her Imagination Library, founded in 1995. Parton’s father was illiterate; it inspired her to launch an organization providing books to those without resources. By 2025, she had given away over 200 million books to children in need.

Parton was truly one of one – a generous country music heroine from the small-town South turned global phenomenon.

“I hope I’ll be remembered as somebody that tried to do some good in the world,” she told The Associated Press in 2024. “And left, you know, a few good things behind.”

(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.personality_title: Dolly Parton’s lasting legacy of music and kindness reaches beyond divides
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dolly Parton was a famous American singer, songwriter, and actress known for her country music and big personality. She grew up poor in rural Tennessee and became a beloved figure across many different groups of people.

**What happened** – Dolly Parton passed away recently, leaving behind a rich legacy. She wrote famous songs like "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You," acted in movies, and built Dollywood, a theme park that helps her local community. She also started charities focused on helping children stay in school, providing books to kids, supporting families after disasters, protecting animals, and funding medical research.

**Impact** – Parton’s work went beyond entertainment. She helped people from all backgrounds, showing kindness and support without taking sides in politics. Her Imagination Library alone has given over 200 million books to children who might not otherwise have them. Her efforts helped improve education, health, and local economies, making a real difference in many lives.

**What's next step** – Her charities will continue to operate and grow, helping new generations. Dollywood remains a major attraction supporting jobs and tourism. Her music and story inspire others to use their talents and resources to help people, proving that one person’s kindness can last a long time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Dolly Parton’s life combined creativity and generosity to build a legacy that brings joy and support across communities.

articles.title: Baltimore reimagines what 911 can do, with $400 million to back it up
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In March, mental health clinician Michala Williams met a 38-year-old woman sobbing in the front seat of her car in a McDonald’s parking lot. The woman had called 911. She had children ranging from age two to 22, a fiancé recently jailed, health issues she was managing alone, and […]
The post Baltimore reimagines what 911 can do, with $400 million to back it up first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

In March, mental health clinician Michala Williams met a 38-year-old woman sobbing in the front seat of her car in a McDonald’s parking lot. The woman had called 911. She had children ranging from age two to 22, a fiancé recently jailed, health issues she was managing alone, and she hadn’t been able to eat. The month before, she’d tried to drive herself to the hospital and gotten pulled over for an expired registration. The officer arrested her for acting erratically. Instead of the hospital, she went to a holding cell.

By the time Williams arrived, the woman had been through the emergency system twice without getting anything from it. By the time Williams left, about an hour later, she had referrals to a psychiatrist, a therapist, legal aid, and a case manager to help determine whether her child with autism qualified for government services.

“She’s been through a lot of trauma, and no one is going to deny that,” Williams said. “But I now have to take all of that and decide, ‘OK, here’s steps 1, 2, and 3,’ because we got to find a little bit of sliver of something to give her some hope that there’s help out here.”

The calls that don’t need a badge

Baltimore fielded 1.68 million calls to 911 in 2024. Many of them, tens of thousands, didn’t require police, fire, or emergency medical services. Someone fell asleep in a store. Someone seemed confused in a park. Someone was yelling at people on the street. Situations where, as Georgetown Law community safety expert Tahir Duckett puts it, a badge and handcuffs are not what the situation needs.

Too often, those calls still result in arrest, cycling the person through the criminal justice system rather than connecting them to housing, mental health care, or addiction treatment.

Baltimore already runs mobile crisis teams through Behavioral Health System Baltimore, a nonprofit that acts as the city’s mental health department. The teams pair a clinician with a peer counselor and respond to mental health calls in place of police. Now the city is expanding that model to cover a broader range of non-emergency situations, around the clock, seven days a week.

How opioid settlement money is funding it

The expansion draws from roughly $400 million Baltimore has received from opioid-related legal settlements. In 2018, the city opted out of a global settlement with opioid makers and distributors and sued them independently. City officials have since committed those funds to drug-related harms and harm-prevention services: housing, healthcare, education.

Baltimore’s homicide rate fell 60 percent from 2021 to 2025, which made national news. Less covered: roughly 1,000 people a year died of overdose over that same stretch. Violence and addiction run through the same communities, and the program is built on the idea that you have to address both.

What the Durham model shows

Durham, North Carolina, has been running a similar program since 2021. The Holistic Empathetic Assistance Response Team, or HEART, has handled more than 12,000 diverted calls over four years. Police backup was needed for 0.02 percent of them. Response times across all call types improved after the program launched.

The Durham call logs tell you something about the gap this is filling. A hotel manager called 911 because a blind guest needed an accessible room; HEART responders booked the room and arranged a ride to a housing organization the next morning. A domestic violence survivor needed somewhere safe to go. A homeless veteran needed a doctor’s appointment. These situations do not require a police officer.

A separate study found that non-law-enforcement responses led to fewer arrests than police responses, with the strongest effect for Black callers, men, and people ages 25 to 39.

Rebecca Neusteter, who leads the Health Lab at the University of Chicago and studies programs like these, says callers get confidence that the right person is coming, and that responders do better work when they can actually solve something. “We also see responders themselves feeling like they have a better toolbox in their ability to pursue actual resolution to these calls,” she said. Nobody’s arguing that police shouldn’t respond to violence. The real question is who might be better suited to respond to the range of cases that make up everything else.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News
articles.reasoning: The article describes Baltimore's innovative and well-funded expansion of non-police 911 response teams to address mental health, addiction, and social service needs, reducing unnecessary arrests and improving community outcomes. This represents a significant, positive real-world impact on public safety and social justice with broad societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: Baltimore uses $400 million to transform 911 with mental health and social support teams
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Baltimore receives nearly 1.7 million 911 calls each year, many of which do not need police or emergency medical help. Instead, these calls often involve people who need mental health care, housing support, or other non-criminal assistance.

**What happened** – The city is expanding a program that sends mental health clinicians and peer counselors—rather than police—to respond to non-emergency 911 calls. This expansion is funded by about $400 million from opioid lawsuit settlements. The new teams work 24/7 and help people connect to services like therapy, legal aid, and housing.

**Impact** – This program helps avoid unnecessary arrests and jail time for people struggling with mental health or addiction issues. For example, a woman who had been arrested after trying to get hospital help was instead connected to support services by a clinician. Similar programs, like one in Durham, North Carolina, have successfully handled thousands of calls with almost no need for police backup. This shows that many problems can be solved without law enforcement, improving outcomes for individuals and communities.

**What's next step** – Baltimore will continue to develop and expand these non-police response teams. The city aims to reduce harm related to addiction and violence by addressing the root causes through health and social services. Other cities may look to Baltimore’s model when updating their emergency response systems.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Baltimore is using opioid settlement money to fund mental health and support teams that respond to 911 calls without police, helping people get the right care and reducing unnecessary arrests.
articles.personality_title_fr: Baltimore utilise 400 millions de dollars pour transformer le 911 avec des équipes de soutien en santé mentale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Baltimore reçoit près de 1,7 million d’appels au 911 chaque année, dont beaucoup ne nécessitent pas l’intervention de la police ou des services médicaux d’urgence. Ces appels concernent souvent des personnes ayant besoin d’aide en santé mentale, de logement ou d’autres soutiens non liés au crime.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La ville étend un programme qui envoie des cliniciens en santé mentale et des conseillers pairs, plutôt que la police, pour répondre aux appels non urgents du 911. Cette extension est financée par environ 400 millions de dollars issus de règlements judiciaires liés aux opioïdes. Les nouvelles équipes travaillent 24 heures sur 24 et aident les personnes à accéder à des services comme la thérapie, l’aide juridique et le logement.

**Impact** – Ce programme évite des arrestations et détentions inutiles pour les personnes en difficulté mentale ou dépendantes. Par exemple, une femme arrêtée après avoir essayé d’obtenir de l’aide à l’hôpital a été orientée vers des services de soutien par une clinicienne. Des programmes similaires, comme celui de Durham en Caroline du Nord, ont réussi à gérer des milliers d’appels avec presque aucun besoin d’intervention policière. Cela montre que de nombreux problèmes peuvent être résolus sans la police, améliorant les résultats pour les individus et les communautés.

**Prochaine étape** – Baltimore va continuer à développer et étendre ces équipes de réponse sans police. La ville vise à réduire les dommages liés à la toxicomanie et à la violence en s’attaquant aux causes profondes via des services de santé et sociaux. D’autres villes pourraient s’inspirer du modèle de Baltimore pour moderniser leurs systèmes d’urgence.

**En une phrase** – Baltimore utilise l’argent des règlements liés aux opioïdes pour financer des équipes de santé mentale qui répondent aux appels du 911 sans police, aidant les personnes à obtenir les soins adaptés et réduisant les arrestations inutiles.
articles.personality_title_es: Baltimore usa 400 millones de dólares para transformar el 911 con equipos de apoyo en salud mental
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Baltimore recibe casi 1.7 millones de llamadas al 911 cada año, muchas de las cuales no requieren policía ni servicios médicos de emergencia. Estas llamadas suelen ser de personas que necesitan apoyo en salud mental, vivienda u otros servicios sociales, no relacionados con delitos.

**Qué pasó** – La ciudad está ampliando un programa que envía clínicos en salud mental y consejeros pares, en lugar de policías, para responder a llamadas no urgentes al 911. Esta expansión se financia con unos 400 millones de dólares provenientes de acuerdos legales por la crisis de opioides. Los nuevos equipos trabajan las 24 horas y ayudan a conectar a las personas con servicios como terapia, ayuda legal y vivienda.

**Impacto** – Este programa ayuda a evitar arrestos y encarcelamientos innecesarios para personas con problemas de salud mental o adicción. Por ejemplo, una mujer que fue arrestada tras intentar buscar ayuda hospitalaria fue conectada a servicios de apoyo por una clínica. Programas similares, como el de Durham, Carolina del Norte, han manejado miles de llamadas con casi ninguna necesidad de respaldo policial. Esto demuestra que muchos problemas se pueden resolver sin policías, mejorando los resultados para las personas y las comunidades.

**Próximo paso** – Baltimore seguirá desarrollando y ampliando estos equipos de respuesta sin policía. La ciudad busca reducir daños relacionados con la adicción y la violencia al abordar las causas principales mediante servicios de salud y sociales. Otras ciudades podrían seguir el ejemplo de Baltimore para modernizar sus sistemas de emergencia.

**Resumen en una frase** – Baltimore usa dinero de acuerdos por opioides para financiar equipos de salud mental que responden al 911 sin policía, ayudando a las personas a recibir la atención correcta y reduciendo arrestos innecesarios.

articles.title: Explainer: UN peace operations work to create, preserve peace
articles.summary: Supporting the first democratic elections after brutal civil wars in Mozambique and Cambodia. Disarming thousands of child soldiers in Sierra Leone. Helping to secure Namibia’s independence from South Africa. These are some of the contributions of UN operations around the world to help countries transition from conflict to lasting peace.
articles.content:
As the world faces the highest number of conflicts since 1945 and a rising death toll from war alongside peace operations increasingly deployed to contain violence rather than implement agreements, the UN and its Member States must adapt to ensure these missions remain relevant, Secretary-General António Guterres told the General Assembly on Wednesday.

“UN peace operations are indispensable tools for maintaining international peace and security, but to be more effective, they must adapt to new realities,” Mr. Guterres said.

At UN Headquarters in New York, the Secretary-General presented the first ever review on the future of all forms of UN peace operations at the request of the landmark Pact for the Future and offered recommendations for the consideration of Member States on how the UN toolbox can be adapted to meet evolving needs and future challenges.

What are UN peace operations?

The Secretary-General’s review covers the wide spectrum of UN peace operations. That includes civilian special political missions and peace enforcement operations authorised by the Security Council – from a two-person office supporting a Personal Envoy to large, multidimensional peacekeeping operations.

“United Nations peace operations are a critical form of multilateral action,” Mr. Guterres said.

“They help defuse crises, stop conflict, sustain ceasefires and protect civilians. In lands stained by bloodshed, they create space for dialogue and open pathways to peace.”

‘Blue Helmet’ landscape

Since 1948, the Council has been authorising UN peacekeepers to help conflict parties reach political solutions, prevent disputes from devolving into conflicts and reduce armed violence while the search for a political solution continues, with 11 active missions.

Known colloquially as “Blue Helmets” for their distinctive uniform, UN peacekeepers are guided by three main principles: there must be consent of the parties to the conflict, impartiality and non-use of force except in self-defence or defence of their mandate.

Their work can be dangerous – more than 4,500 UN peacekeepers have died in missions around the world – and their efforts have been widely recognised, including when they collectively received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988 “for preventing armed clashes and creating conditions for negotiations”.

Special political missions

Special political missions comprise civilian personnel deployed based on mandates from the Security Council to prevent conflicts, mediate peace discussions and support political transitions.

They do not rely on large military or armed forces, but instead work with governments, conflict parties, regional organizations and civil society.

The UN has deployed 167 such missions since 1948, with about 40 active in 2024, according to a review by the UN’s Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs.

UNSMIL

Peace enforcement

The Security Council authorises peace enforcement operations under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which mandates them to apply a range of measures, including the use of military force.

Unlike peacekeeping and special political missions, peace enforcement does not always require the consent of the conflict parties, and “Blue Helmets” do not directly participate.

In a number of recent settings, such as Haiti, Mali and Somalia, UN peace missions have operated alongside Council-authorised peace enforcement operations by non-UN forces, carrying out mandates focused on supporting national political processes and wider peace consolidation tasks.

Council-mandated peace support operations deployed by the African Union also fall under this category.

Current state of affairs

The current operating environment for peace operations has deteriorated, the UN chief warned in his review.

Tweet URL

Conflicts have become more complex, comprehensive peace agreements are less common and funding has declined, with recent cuts slashing nearly half a billion dollars for peacekeeping and $96.3 million for special political missions, according to the report.

For Mr. Guterres, peace operations cannot serve as an alternative for political will by the involved parties to end a conflict, although some current missions operate amid deadlocked talks and high violence.

“No peace operation and no political process supported by the United Nations can succeed without solid and cohesive support from Member States,” he said.

From drones to disinformation

Mr. Guterres said mission mandates for peace operations must be narrowly focused with achievable objectives, adaptable, cost-efficient, accountable – especially involving claims of sexual exploitation and abuse – and cooperative with Member States and UN offices.

In practice, adaptation would mean more than rewriting mandates. The report calls for lighter and more mobile mission footprints, stronger data and threat analysis, technology to counter drones and disinformation and more measures to ensure peacekeepers’ safety.

Mr. Guterres identified missions focused on peace in Colombia and a border dispute between Cameroon and Nigeria as examples of what peace operations can achieve under the right conditions.

Looking into the future

The Secretary-General’s review also contains dozens of recommendations to “reset peace operations for a new geopolitical era”, one marked by more wars, significant financial constraints and fragmented support for peacekeeping missions.

Recommendations include:

Prioritising the creation of conditions for political processes to advance

Deploying missions only around credible political purposes

Strengthening partnerships with host States

Clarifying the division of labour between UN agencies

Planning exit strategies and transition plans at the outset

Above all, the future of UN peace operations relies on Member States’ continued belief that despite their flaws, they remain essential instruments of creating the conditions to end conflicts, according to the UN chief.

“Together, we must build a shared vision of what each mission can achieve throughout its life cycle,” Mr. Guterres said.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: UN peace operations adapt to protect and build lasting peace worldwide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Since 1948, the United Nations (UN) has sent peace operations to help countries recover from wars and conflicts. These missions include peacekeepers, political teams, and enforcement groups that support peace talks, protect civilians, and help with elections.

**What happened** – UN Secretary-General António Guterres presented the first full review of all UN peace operations. He explained how these missions work today, the challenges they face, and how they must change to stay effective. The review was shared with UN Member States during a recent meeting at the UN headquarters in New York.

**Impact** – UN peace operations have helped countries like Mozambique, Cambodia, Sierra Leone, and Namibia move from war to peace. They protect people, stop fighting, and create chances for dialogue. But conflicts are now more complex, and funding has decreased. The review shows that peace missions must become quicker, smarter, and better at handling new threats like drones and false information.

**What's next step** – The UN plans to make peace operations more flexible and focused. This includes using new technology, improving safety for peacekeepers, and working closely with countries involved. The UN also wants Member States to support these efforts strongly and plan how missions will end once peace is secured.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN is updating its peace missions to better handle today’s conflicts and help countries build lasting peace with stronger support and smarter tools.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les opérations de paix de l’ONU évoluent pour protéger et construire une paix durable dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 1948, les Nations Unies (ONU) envoient des opérations de paix pour aider les pays à se remettre des guerres et des conflits. Ces missions comprennent des casques bleus, des équipes politiques et des groupes d’application qui soutiennent les négociations de paix, protègent les civils et aident aux élections.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a présenté la première revue complète de toutes les opérations de paix de l’ONU. Il a expliqué comment ces missions fonctionnent aujourd’hui, les défis qu’elles rencontrent et comment elles doivent évoluer pour rester efficaces. La revue a été partagée avec les États membres lors d’une réunion récente au siège de l’ONU à New York.

**Impact** – Les opérations de paix de l’ONU ont aidé des pays comme le Mozambique, le Cambodge, la Sierra Leone et la Namibie à passer de la guerre à la paix. Elles protègent les populations, stoppent les combats et créent des opportunités de dialogue. Mais les conflits sont aujourd’hui plus complexes et le financement a diminué. La revue montre que les missions doivent devenir plus rapides, plus intelligentes et mieux équipées pour faire face à de nouvelles menaces comme les drones et la désinformation.

**Prochaines étapes** – L’ONU prévoit de rendre les opérations de paix plus flexibles et ciblées. Cela inclut l’utilisation de nouvelles technologies, l’amélioration de la sécurité des casques bleus et une coopération étroite avec les pays concernés. L’ONU souhaite aussi que les États membres soutiennent fortement ces efforts et planifient la fin des missions une fois la paix assurée.

**Phrase-clé** – L’ONU modernise ses missions de paix pour mieux gérer les conflits actuels et aider les pays à construire une paix durable grâce à un soutien renforcé et des outils plus performants.
articles.personality_title_es: Las operaciones de paz de la ONU se adaptan para proteger y construir una paz duradera en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde 1948, las Naciones Unidas (ONU) han enviado operaciones de paz para ayudar a los países a recuperarse de guerras y conflictos. Estas misiones incluyen cascos azules, equipos políticos y grupos de aplicación que apoyan negociaciones de paz, protegen a civiles y ayudan con elecciones.

**Qué pasó** – El Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, presentó la primera revisión completa de todas las operaciones de paz de la ONU. Explicó cómo funcionan estas misiones hoy, los retos que enfrentan y cómo deben cambiar para seguir siendo efectivas. La revisión se compartió con los Estados Miembros en una reunión reciente en la sede de la ONU en Nueva York.

**Impacto** – Las operaciones de paz de la ONU han ayudado a países como Mozambique, Camboya, Sierra Leona y Namibia a pasar de la guerra a la paz. Protegen a las personas, detienen los combates y crean oportunidades para el diálogo. Pero los conflictos son ahora más complejos y la financiación ha disminuido. La revisión muestra que las misiones deben ser más rápidas, inteligentes y estar mejor preparadas para enfrentar nuevas amenazas como drones y desinformación.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU planea hacer que las operaciones de paz sean más flexibles y enfocadas. Esto incluye usar nueva tecnología, mejorar la seguridad de los cascos azules y trabajar de cerca con los países involucrados. La ONU también quiere que los Estados Miembros apoyen fuertemente estos esfuerzos y planifiquen cómo terminarán las misiones una vez que se asegure la paz.

**Una frase clave** – La ONU está actualizando sus misiones de paz para manejar mejor los conflictos actuales y ayudar a los países a construir una paz duradera con más apoyo y mejores herramientas.

articles.title: How Buryat fashion designer Oksana Alkhunsaeva stitched her life back together in Russia
articles.summary: Oksana was the youngest child in the Khunkheev family — a Buryat family. At school, classmates mocked her surname and appearance. Now a successful designer, she still thinks about the trauma.
articles.content:
This article was first published in Russian by online Russian media Potok and Novaya Vkladka on May 11, 2026. Global Voices translated it into English, edited it for clarity, and is republishing it with permission from Potok and Novaya Vkladka. This post is also part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

One night, Oksana had a dream. She dreamed of her late grandmother. In the dream, her grandmother said just one word: “Sew.” Today, outfits by Buryat costume designer Oksana Alkhunsaeva are ordered from all over Russia: from Moscow and St. Petersburg to Yakutsk and Kamchatka.

Oksana was the youngest child in the Khunkheev family, a Buryat family. She was born in 1984 in Ust-Ordynsky, a settlement of about 15,000 people in the Irkutsk region. She was a long-awaited daughter, born after two boys. Her parents’ family observed traditional rituals and spoke Buryat, even though that was not customary at the time. Oksana recalls that from childhood she “saw everything Buryat” and that “everything was done as though that was simply the natural way things should be.”

The Buryats are a Mongolic people, indigenous to the Lake Baikal region. Historically, they formed part of the wider Mongol cultural and political world, while retaining numerous Mongol clan and tribal identities. Traditionally, they constituted the major northern subgroup of the Mongols.

Russian colonization of these parts of Siberia began around the 1620s, with the forceful military advance of the Russian army — Cossacks at the time — and their conquest of the East of Siberia. They built fortresses, imposed tributes (with the Buryats being made to pay regular fees to the Russians), and eventually displaced existing political ties with Mongol rulers. Buryat communities repeatedly resisted, attacked Russian positions, or fled south into Mongolia before Russian authority was established through the late 17th and early 18th centuries.

Under the Russian Empire and especially the Soviet Union, colonial integration deepened through land and economic redistribution, collectivization, repression of Buddhist institutions and Buryat elites, and increasing cultural Russification. Soviet authorities also removed “Mongol” from the republic’s name in 1958.

Today, most Buryats remain within the Russian Federation, particularly in the Republic of Buryatia. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Buryatia has also reportedly experienced disproportionately high military casualties and mobilization. Independent media outlet Ludi Baikala counted 9,200 people from Buryatia and the Irkutsk region killed in the 2022–2026 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

In the context of this history, the Khunkheev family did not wear traditional clothing in everyday life, but Oksana’s grandmother had real gutuls (Buryat boots). Oksana loved both clothing and sewing from an early age. She played with dolls and imagined herself as a fashion designer, inventing patterns and making clothes for them. She watched the then-popular TV series “Simply Maria” (“Simplemente Maria”), in which an ordinary Mexican girl moves from a remote rural province to the capital, Mexico City, to become a designer. Little Oksana from Ust-Ordynsky dreamed of the same thing.

Her teenage years were difficult. In eighth grade, she transferred to a new school and immediately became an outcast. She was used to her brothers protecting her and her father calling her his “beauty.” But at school, classmates mocked her full lips, twisted her surname into insults, and kicked her bag of textbooks down the corridors. Oksana learned to shut herself off; even today, any conflict triggers what she calls a delayed-reaction syndrome. The pain and hurt do not hit immediately; they come hours or days later, and are very difficult to process. Wanting to understand why people behave this way, she went on to earn a university degree in psychology.

It was by chance that Oksana came to work at the Center for the Preservation and Development of the Buryat Ethnic Group. In 2008, when she joined, the Center was organizing the Altargana festival in Irkutsk.

This festival for Buryat communities was first held in Mongolia in 1994. Since then, it has become international in scope and grown into a large-scale event attended by people from across the globe — from Inner Mongolia in China to France. Oksana was completely astonished both by its scale and by what she saw there.

“Before that, I had barely seen our national clothing. But at the festival, all the richness of Buryat traditions was there at once. I watched and admired it,” she recalls.

The festival is named after the altargana plant, which, with its small leaves and modest golden-yellow flowers, looks humble but has an incredibly well-developed root system. Oksana thought a great deal about her own roots and then understood what exactly she wanted to create — but she was still a long way from that point.

After her second maternity leave, Oksana worked sales and other jobs unrelated to sewing. She could only sew late in the evening, when the workday was over, and her children were asleep, but dreams were never something abstract to her; she always paid attention to whatever came to her in that way.

She had a sewing machine she had won in a competition; there was a piece of fabric lying around, the children fell asleep at ten, and late at night, she had a little free time. Oksana knew that she needed to sew, but didn’t know how. She made her first costumes for relatives and loved ones, as she wanted her children, nieces, and nephews to wear national clothing and take an interest in their culture.

The results began to look beautiful, but they turned out to be too traditional: Clothing made strictly “according to the canon” simply had nowhere to be worn. She also wanted recognition and visibility, so Oksana tried to participate in different fashion shows. At one of them, a journalist approached her and asked for an interview; it was exactly the way Oksana had seen it happen in “Simply Maria.”

Although the runway, bright lights, and professional models looked like the dream she had imagined as a child, over time Oksana has come to see that her main aspiration is for people to wear her clothes. Still, she adds that she was named best designer in the Ust-Orda Buryat district in 2023.

For her, a Buryat costume is not a museum exhibit; it is important to see the person and begin the work with that individual. First, she tries to understand what shapes and silhouettes the client likes in ordinary clothing, and only then does she “translate” those preferences into the language of Buryat costume.

Now, Oksana’s entire family works together. Her husband is the organizer; her mother helps at fashion shows, irons garments, and finishes urgent sewing; her father makes special knives and drives everyone where they need to go. Her mother-in-law and sister-in-law help as well.

Laughing, Oksana admits that she sometimes wants to go back to a calm, stable office life — but when people approach her and ask, “How can I find a costume like yours?” she realizes that every time thoughts of leaving enter her mind, life seems to deliberately send her a sign: “It’s as though someone won’t let me go and keeps saying, ‘Sew.’”

articles.personality_title: Buryat designer Oksana Alkhunsaeva brings traditional clothing to life in modern Russia
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva is from the Buryat people, an indigenous group in Siberia with a rich history. For many years, Buryat culture faced challenges due to Russian colonization and the Soviet Union’s efforts to change local traditions. Growing up, Oksana experienced bullying because of her background and appearance.

**What happened** – Inspired by a dream of her grandmother’s advice to “sew,” Oksana began making traditional Buryat costumes. Starting late at night after her children slept, she created clothes for family and then showed her work at fashion shows. Over time, she became a well-known designer across Russia, blending traditional styles with modern tastes. Her whole family now helps with her work.

**Impact** – Oksana’s work is important because it helps keep Buryat culture alive in everyday life, not just in museums. By mixing old designs with new fashion, she makes traditional clothing something people want to wear today. This helps Buryat people feel proud of their culture and shares their heritage with others.

**What’s next step** – Oksana plans to keep creating clothes that fit modern styles while honoring Buryat traditions. She wants more people to wear her designs and learn about her culture. Her family’s support means her work can grow even bigger in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva turned childhood struggles into a creative mission to revive and modernize Buryat clothing, celebrating her culture through fashion.
articles.personality_title_fr: La créatrice bouriate Oksana Alkhunsaeva fait revivre les vêtements traditionnels en Russie moderne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva vient du peuple bouriate, un groupe indigène de Sibérie avec une histoire riche. Pendant longtemps, la culture bouriate a été mise à mal par la colonisation russe et les efforts soviétiques pour changer les traditions locales. En grandissant, Oksana a été victime d’intimidation à cause de ses origines et de son apparence.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Inspirée par un rêve où sa grand-mère lui disait de « coudre », Oksana a commencé à créer des costumes traditionnels bouriats. Elle cousait tard la nuit après que ses enfants soient endormis, confectionnant des vêtements pour sa famille, puis a présenté ses créations lors de défilés de mode. Avec le temps, elle est devenue une créatrice reconnue en Russie, mêlant styles anciens et goûts modernes. Toute sa famille l’aide désormais.

**Impact** – Le travail d’Oksana est important car il permet de garder la culture bouriate vivante dans la vie quotidienne, pas seulement dans les musées. En mélangeant les anciens motifs avec la mode actuelle, elle rend les vêtements traditionnels désirables aujourd’hui. Cela renforce la fierté culturelle bouriate et fait connaître leur héritage.

**Prochaine étape** – Oksana souhaite continuer à créer des vêtements qui allient styles modernes et traditions bouriates. Elle veut que plus de personnes portent ses créations et découvrent sa culture. Le soutien de sa famille permettra à son travail de grandir encore.

**Phrase clé** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva a transformé ses difficultés d’enfance en une mission créative pour faire revivre et moderniser les vêtements bouriats, célébrant sa culture à travers la mode.
articles.personality_title_es: La diseñadora buriata Oksana Alkhunsaeva revive la ropa tradicional en la Rusia moderna
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva es del pueblo buriato, un grupo indígena de Siberia con una historia rica. Durante mucho tiempo, la cultura buriata enfrentó dificultades debido a la colonización rusa y los esfuerzos soviéticos por cambiar las tradiciones locales. De niña, Oksana sufrió burlas por su origen y apariencia.

**Qué pasó** – Inspirada por un sueño en el que su abuela le decía “cose”, Oksana comenzó a hacer trajes tradicionales buriatos. Cosía de noche, después de que sus hijos dormían, creando ropa para su familia y luego mostrando su trabajo en desfiles de moda. Con el tiempo, se volvió una diseñadora reconocida en Rusia, combinando estilos antiguos con gustos modernos. Toda su familia ahora la ayuda.

**Impacto** – El trabajo de Oksana es importante porque mantiene viva la cultura buriata en la vida diaria, no solo en museos. Al mezclar diseños antiguos con moda actual, hace que la ropa tradicional sea atractiva hoy. Esto ayuda a que el pueblo buriato se sienta orgulloso de su cultura y comparte su herencia.

**Próximo paso** – Oksana planea seguir creando ropa que combine estilos modernos y tradiciones buriatas. Quiere que más personas usen sus diseños y conozcan su cultura. El apoyo de su familia permitirá que su trabajo crezca aún más.

**Frase clave** – Oksana Alkhunsaeva convirtió sus dificultades de infancia en una misión creativa para revivir y modernizar la ropa buriata, celebrando su cultura a través de la moda.
